name: Akihud
title: Son of Ehud in the tribe of Benjamin
summary: Ahihud belonged to the tribe of Benjamin and was the son of Ehud, a Benjamite clan leader mentioned in 1 Chronicles 8. He is named in verse 7 along with his brothers Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera. According to the biblical text, he and his brothers were taken captive to Manahath, a settlement southwest of Jerusalem, reflecting internal movements among Benjamin's descendants. The Ehud mentioned here should probably not be confused with the well-known judge Ehud son of Gera in the book of Judges. Ahihud's presence in the genealogy testifies to the Chroniclers' care in preserving and documenting even the least known branches of Israel's tribal history.

keyEvents.title: Mentioned in the genealogy of Benjamin
keyEvents.description: Akihud is listed as one of the sons of Ehud in the genealogy of the tribe of Benjamin in 1 Chronicles.

keyEvents.title: Taken to Manahat
keyEvents.description: According to the text, Akihud and his brothers were taken to Manahat, a settlement southwest of Jerusalem. This indicates an internal relocation or forced migration among the descendants of Benjamin.

versions.summary: Akihud was a descendant of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in 1 Chronicles as part of the genealogies. He was the son of Ehud and belonged to one of the prominent families in the tribe of Benjamin. His role in the Bible is primarily genealogical, contributing to tracing the lineage of the tribe of Benjamin.
versions.title: Descendant of Benjamin
versions.reason: [critical] Ahihud lived in the later history of the tribe of Benjamin, not in the time of the patriarchs. The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 8 cover periods long after the patriarchs. Ehud (his father) and the context of being taken to Manahat place him likely in the period of the judges or the early monarchy. 'judges' or 'united-kingdom' are more appropriate eras.; [major] There is no biblical evidence that Ahihud was a 'leader'. He is mentioned only in a genealogy. A more fitting role would be 'ancestor' or 'link in the lineage of the tribe of Benjamin'. Calling him a 'leader' is speculative.; [major] According to 1 Chronicles 8:6-7, Ahihud is listed together with Naaman and Ahijah as sons of Ehud. The other names (Abishua, Ahoah, Gera, Shupham, Huram) belong to other branches or generations in the genealogy of Benjamin and are not necessarily siblings of Ahihud. The list of siblings should be corrected to those actually mentioned as sons of Ehud in the verse.; [minor] The summary is acceptable but should clarify that the Ehud in 1 Chronicles 8:6 is not necessarily the same Ehud as the judge in the Book of Judges. It should also mention the relocation to Manahat as an important detail.; [minor] The fourth key event ('Preservation of the genealogies') is more a theological reflection than a concrete event connected to Ahihud. It may be kept, but the wording should be made more restrained.; [minor] There are no footnotes about interesting details such as the place name Manahat, the relationship between this Ehud and the judge Ehud, and the linguistic meaning of the name Ahihud.

versions.summary: Akihud was a descendant of the tribe of Benjamin, mentioned in 1 Chronicles as part of the genealogies. He was the son of Ehud (not necessarily identical to the judge Ehud) and belonged to one of the families of the tribe of Benjamin. According to the text, he and his brothers were taken captive to Manahat, which testifies to internal movements among Benjamin's descendants. His role in the Bible is primarily genealogical, contributing to documenting the lineage of the tribe of Benjamin.
versions.title: Descendant of Ehud in the Tribe of Benjamin
versions.reason: [major] According to 1 Chr 8:7, it is Naaman, Ahia and Gera who are mentioned in connection with Ehud. 'Ahia' should probably be written as 'ahia' (lowercase id), but more importantly: Gera is also mentioned in the context as the one who carried them away. Depending on interpretation, siblings may include gera. Furthermore, siblings should consistently use lowercase id format.; [minor] The summary is good, but there is some overlap with version 1. The text should be rephrased more clearly to distinguish it from the previous version and provide greater precision regarding the context in 1 Chr 8:6-7.; [minor] Era 'judges' is uncertain. Akihud is only mentioned in the genealogies of 1 Chronicles, and it is not clear that he lived during the period of the judges. Since he is a genealogical figure without specific dating, both 'judges' or 'united-kingdom' can be defended, but the uncertainty should be noted.; [minor] The role 'patriarch' is somewhat imprecise since it is not stated that Akihud had descendants in the text. A more accurate role would be 'family head' or simply 'mentioned in the genealogy'.; [minor] The third key event ('Part of Benjamin's tribal family history') is very general and overlaps with the first. It could usefully be tightened or removed.; [major] In 1 Chr 8:7, Naaman, Ahia and Gera are mentioned in connection with the abduction to Manahat. Gera should be considered part of the sibling list. The current list may possibly lack 'gera'.; [minor] The linguistic footnote gives two possible meanings of the name. 'Brother of wonder' is a more speculative etymology. A more recognized interpretation is 'my brother is majesty/grandeur' (אחי + הוד). This should be clarified.

versions.summary: Akihud was the son of Ehud and belonged to the tribe of Benjamin. He is known exclusively from the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 8, where he is mentioned together with his brothers Naaman, Ahijah, and Gera. According to the text, he and his brothers were taken captive to Manahat, a place southwest of Jerusalem, which testifies to internal movements among Benjamin's descendants. The Ehud mentioned as his father is likely not identical to the judge Ehud son of Gera from the book of Judges. Akihud's role in Scripture is genealogical, and his name helps document and preserve the family lines of the tribe of Benjamin through the generations.
versions.title: Son of Ehud in the tribe of Benjamin
versions.reason: [major] Ahihud is known from the genealogy in 1 Chronicles 8, which was compiled after the exile. Although the person may have lived during the period of the judges, this is uncertain. The time periods 'divided-kingdom' or 'return' could also be relevant, but given that Ehud (his father) is placed in an early Benjaminite context and the text refers to events that seem to be from pre-monarchic or early monarchic times, 'judges' is acceptable but uncertain. Keep 'judges' but note the uncertainty.; [minor] The role 'clan leader' is somewhat speculative. The text mentions Ahihud as the son of Ehud but gives no explicit indication that he was a clan leader. A more neutral role such as 'tribal member' or 'mentioned in the genealogy' might be more precise.; [minor] In 1 Chron 8:7, Naaman, Ahijah and Gera are mentioned together with Ahihud, but there is textual-critical debate about who carried off whom, and whether Gera was a brother or another person in this context. The text is difficult to interpret, but the current list is a reasonable reading.; [minor] The summary is good and informative, but there have been two earlier versions with similar introductions. To avoid repetition and further improve quality, the wording could be tightened somewhat and made more distinct.

footnotes.text: The name Akihud (Hebrew: אֲחִיחוּד, Ahihud) is composed of אָח (ach, 'brother') and הוֹד (hod, 'majesty/grandeur'), and can be translated as 'my brother is majestic' or 'brother to greatness'. This form of the name appears only in 1 Chronicles 8:7.

Manahat, the place to which Akihud's family was taken captive, is generally identified with Malha (modern Manahat), a village southwest of Jerusalem. Archaeological excavations have uncovered settlement traces from the Iron Age in this area, confirming that it was an established settlement in biblical times.

Ehud mentioned in 1 Chronicles 8:6 as the father of Akihud is most likely not identical to the judge Ehud son of Gera from Judges 3:15–30. The genealogies in Chronicles contain several individuals with the same name across generations, and the context points to a different person.

The genealogies in 1 Chronicles 1–9 were probably compiled after the Babylonian exile and served an important function in restoring tribal identity, legitimizing property rights, and confirming belonging to God's people. The preservation of even less well-known names like Akihud underscores the biblical value of documenting every single lineage.

The captivity to Manahat mentioned in 1 Chron 8:6–7 is an example of internal movements among the tribes of Israel. Such forced relocations could be due to tribal conflicts, land distribution, or political circumstances, and testify to the dynamics of settlement patterns in ancient Israel.

The verse 1 Chron 8:6–7 is textually challenging. The Hebrew base text is compressed and ambiguous, and there is disagreement among interpreters about who carried out the captivity and exactly which individuals were involved. The Septuagint (LXX) differs somewhat from the Masoretic text on this point.
